rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Jewish objection aimed to cast Islam’s call as a political bid for authority rather than a religious message, undermining it as a reform movement.
rows.anchor: the Prophet (sws)’s call was not that of religion; it is a mere tussle to attain political authority

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says a similar objection by the People of the Book had already been answered in Sūrah al-Ḥadīd.
rows.anchor: similar objection raised by the People of the Book

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hypocrites demanded the Banū Naḍīr assets be divided like war booty; the Qur’an classifies them as fay for the public treasury, especially to aid needy Muslims expelled for their faith.
rows.anchor: The second question was raised by the hypocrites regarding the left-behind assets and wealth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi praises the Anṣār and early Muhājirūn for generosity toward immigrant brothers, preferring their needs over their own; this sacrifice and contentment befit believers.
rows.anchor: the Anṣār and the early Muhājirūn are praised for their sacrifice and contentment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word līnah means a palm tree bearing fruit.
rows.anchor: refers to a fruit-laden palm tree.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Jews turned the Muslims’ cutting of trees during the Banū Naḍīr attack into propaganda, arguing that self-described reformers had ruined valuable orchards.
rows.anchor: The Jews used this incident to launch a propaganda against Islam.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the objection concerned felling trees, mentioning spared trees exposes the added accusation: Muslims chose fruit-bearing trees over less costly ones for revenge and financial harm, not military need.
rows.anchor: they left intact those trees and chopped off the fruit-laden ones, which shows that they did it out of revenge

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The divine-permission phrase answers the charge by addressing Muslims, telling them to disregard the accusers’ supposed advice about which trees to fell.
rows.anchor: instead of being directed to those who had raised the objection, it is addressed to the Muslims only.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the felling was done at the Prophet’s direction, it was by God’s directive; God alone knows its wisdom and whether it serves order or disorder.
rows.anchor: was done in the presence of the Prophet (sws) and at his behest

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The directive also aimed to humiliate covenant-breakers by making them watch helplessly as trees they had carefully planted were cut down.
rows.anchor: so that the Almighty humiliates those who break promises and are traitors

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here fāsiq means a traitor or promise-breaker, a sense Islahi says occurs elsewhere in the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: here refers to a traitor and one who breaks promises

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accusers are not addressed because their emotional objection is unreasonable; Muslims are addressed to ratify the act, grieve the traitors, and warn hypocrites against spreading malicious suggestions.
rows.anchor: the objection was absolutely unreasonable, raised only to vent emotions

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In war Muslims may destroy enemy homes, orchards, or crops when military need requires it; without such need, even minor harm to enemy property is forbidden.
rows.anchor: if the war requires that even their houses be razed to the ground, then they can do it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hypocrites wanted Banū Naḍīr wealth treated as enemy booty and divided four-fifths to soldiers, but Islahi rejects the analogy: Badr involved formal fighting and military service, whereas the Banū Naḍīr left in terror without it.
rows.anchor: In the battle of Badr, soldiers had to engage in a formal war

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fay is enemy wealth acquired without battle and belongs to God’s Messenger, hence the Islamic state, for Islam’s and Muslims’ collective welfare rather than soldier shares.
rows.anchor: all of it will belong to God and His Prophet (sws), or in other words to the Islamic state

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fay became a permanent Islamic-finance term for wealth obtained from an enemy without war.
rows.anchor: It refers to the wealth obtained from the enemy without any war.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fay literally means return: God returns wealth to its rightful owners from those who had embezzled it.
rows.anchor: literally means “to return” ie. the Almighty returned this wealth to its rightful owners

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Soldiers’ share of war spoils was justified by their use of personal weapons, horses, and camels and provision of their own supplies.
rows.anchor: the share given to soldiers from the spoils of war was because they used their personal weapons

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the present situation, Islahi says any wealth obtained from an enemy counts as fay, whether gained through war or a peace settlement.
rows.anchor: whatever will now be obtained from the enemy will be regarded as fay

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi links the Messenger’s divinely granted dominance to 58:21: God can make him prevail over great powers without an army; help from believers grants them blessing and distinguishes the sincere from hypocrites.
rows.anchor: The Almighty has ordained: “I and My messengers shall always prevail,”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After distinguishing fay from war spoils, the verse specifies its spending categories; soldiers receive no share, and the categories parallel those named for spoils in Sūrah al-Anfāl.
rows.anchor: this verse states the heads under which the latter can be spent. In other words, the soldiers will have no share in it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God needs no wealth; the share designated for Him returns to servants and is spent by the Islamic government on the needy and Muslims’ collective welfare.
rows.anchor: He is not in need of any person’s wealth or property. The share allocated for Him, in fact, returns to His servants

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Messenger’s share is for him as head of the Islamic state, not as prophet; after his death it passes to the Muslim ruler, not heirs, because it is public provision rather than private inheritance.
rows.anchor: it is allocated to him in his capacity as the head of an Islamic state

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God undertook to provide for the Prophet in his prophetic capacity; once he led a state, its administration required support from the public treasury.
rows.anchor: the Almighty had taken upon Himself to financially provide for Him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The relatives are those of the Prophet for whose financial maintenance he was responsible.
rows.anchor: This refers to those relatives of the Prophet (sws) to whom he was responsible to provide for financially.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The relatives’ support was not their family’s private property or a basis for monopoly over the public treasury; Islahi calls such claims baseless and says miscreants under Jewish influence spread them.
rows.anchor: neither did a particular family ever hold a monopoly on the public treasury, nor can it ever do so.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their placement after the Prophet’s relatives marks the government’s primary financial duty to people without means; other state obligations come afterward.
rows.anchor: The primary responsibility of an Islamic government is the financial responsibility of those who have no means in the society.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If government uses public funds for other purposes while neglecting the poor, it usurps their rights; an Islamic government may spend nothing on luxuries or needless things.
rows.anchor: There is absolutely no allowance to an Islamic government to spend a single penny on luxuries and needless things.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi blames governments that neglect these duties for socialism’s rise; he says socialism made private ownership a crime and caused great bloodshed to uproot it.
rows.anchor: the world was inflicted by the scourge called socialism which rendered the concept of private ownership a crime

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dawla means circulation; related usage can mean the changing of times, and mudāwala derives from this root; 3:140 describes vicissitudes alternating among people.
rows.anchor: We alternate these vicissitudes among mankind, (3:140)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The poor, orphans, and people without resources have a fixed public-treasury share so wealth flows to them instead of circulating only among the rich.
rows.anchor: the share of the poor, the orphans and the resourceless has been fixed in the public treasury

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi presents a principle of Islamic economics: wealth should not stay in circulation within a single social section.
rows.anchor: Islam does not want wealth to just circulate in one section of a society; it wants that it should
